findings.description: HTML sanitizer `Cleaner._remove_javascript_link` relies on a whitespace/control-char stripping regex before the javascript-scheme check, which is an incomplete deny-list and known to be bypassable (basis of CVE-2020-27783-class issues in lxml.html.clean).
findings.code_snippet:
def _remove_javascript_link(self, link):
        # links like "j a v a s c r i p t:" might be interpreted in IE
        new = _substitute_whitespace('', unquote_plus(link))
        if _is_javascript_scheme(new):
            # FIXME: should this be None to delete?
            return ''
        return link
findings.reasoning:
This is the URL sanitizer wired into the cleaning pipeline via `doc.rewrite_links(self._remove_javascript_link, resolve_base_href=False)` (clean.py:305). The URL is neutralized only by (a) one `unquote_plus()` pass and (b) deleting characters matching `[\s\x00-\x08\x0B\x0C\x0E-\x19]+`, followed by a regex deny-list `(?:javascript|jscript|livescript|vbscript|data|about|mocha):`.

Concrete gaps:
1. The whitespace/control-character class stops at \x19, so \x1A-\x1F and \x7F are NOT stripped. Browsers/legacy handlers strip or ignore many of these control characters in URL schemes, so `java\x1Ascript:alert(1)` survives `_substitute_whitespace`, and `_is_possibly_malicious_scheme` searches with `re.search` for the literal `javascript:` — with the embedded control char inserted between "java" and "script" the pattern no longer matches and the original, unsanitized `link` is returned.
2. `unquote_plus` is applied only once, so double-encoded input (`%256Aavascript:` → `%6Aavascript:` after one decode) is compared against the deny-list in still-encoded form.
3. Mixed/rare schemes and scheme-relative abuse are not covered by the deny-list; the check is a black list, not an allow list, and only whitespace is normalized.
4. Only attributes known to `rewrite_links` are processed; the `data:image/...;base64` exemption in `_is_image_dataurl` also blanket-allows `data:image/svg+xml;base64,...`.

Because this function is the last line of defense for HTML that applications pass through `Cleaner`/`clean_html`, any bypass results in stored/reflected XSS in the consuming application. Severity is high, but confirming an end-to-end working bypass requires testing against a specific browser/consumer, hence manual review rather than a definitive true positive. Note this whole module was later deprecated by the lxml project precisely because regex-based sanitization like this cannot be made reliable.

def _is_javascript_scheme(s):
    if _is_image_dataurl(s):  # r'^data:image/.+;base64'
        return None
    return _is_possibly_malicious_scheme(s)

Line 305: doc.rewrite_links(self._remove_javascript_link, resolve_base_href=False)

If the black-list regex does not match (e.g. control char \x1A inserted inside the scheme, or double-encoded payload), the ORIGINAL url is returned unchanged and written back into the sanitized document.
evidence.notes: Control-char class in the stripping regex ends at \x19, leaving \x1A-\x1F and \x7F in the string; double unquoting is not performed; deny-list based sanitization. Module deprecated upstream in lxml 5.0 for exactly this class of weakness.

findings.description: `Cleaner._has_sneaky_javascript` decides whether to delete a CSS `style` attribute / `<style>` body based on a regex-plus-whitespace-stripping heuristic; it can be bypassed, allowing CSS/IE `expression()` or smuggled markup to survive sanitization.
findings.reasoning:
This function is the gatekeeper for CSS content at clean.py:310-335: for every element carrying a `style` attribute (and for `<style>` bodies) the cleaner removes `expression(...)`/`@import` occurrences and then calls `_has_sneaky_javascript(new)`; only if this returns True is the style dropped.

The heuristic is pattern based and cannot be complete:
- Comment stripping `/\*.*?\*/` with `re.S` is non-nesting and runs only once; nested constructs such as `expr/**/ession(` or `exp/**/ression(` leave a reconstituted `expression(`, and `_substitute_comments` runs before the backslash removal and whitespace strip, so payloads can be reassembled by the browser after the checks.
- The whitespace/control-character class `[\s\x00-\x08\x0B\x0C\x0E-\x19]+` again leaves \x1A-\x1F and \x7F intact, so `java\x09script:` (fine) but `java\x1Ascript:` (not stripped) evades the plain `'javascript:' in style` substring test.
- `_looks_like_tag_content` uses `re.search(r'</?[a-zA-Z]+|\son[a-zA-Z]+\s*=')`; because all whitespace has already been removed from `style` at that point, the `\son[a-zA-Z]+\s*=` alternative can never match, and tag-name detection only catches a subset of smuggling forms.
- `.lower()` is applied after the backslash removal, so case/escape combinations are only partially handled.

If bypassed, the attacker's CSS/markup survives `Cleaner` and the consuming application renders attacker-controlled style content — XSS in legacy IE (expression()) or CSS-injection-driven exfiltration. Severity high, exploitability depends on the consuming browser/context (legacy vs. modern), so this needs manual review/verification against real payloads rather than a blanket confirmed true positive.

Lines 70-72: _looks_like_tag_content = re.compile(r'</?[a-zA-Z]+|\son[a-zA-Z]+\s*=', ...).search
Line 524: _substitute_comments = re.compile(r'/\*.*?\*/', re.S).sub
Lines 315-335: new = _replace_css_javascript('', old); new = _replace_css_import('', new); if self._has_sneaky_javascript(new): del el.attrib['style'] ... el.text = '/* deleted */'
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Attacker HTML -> Cleaner.clean_html -> fromstring -> Cleaner.__call__ -> for el in _find_styled_elements(doc): old = el.get('style') -> _has_sneaky_javascript(new) -> if False, el.set('style', new) keeps attacker CSS. Same for <style> element text at lines 327-336.
evidence.notes: After whitespace removal the '\son[a-zA-Z]+\s*=' branch of _looks_like_tag_content is unreachable; whitespace class excludes \x1A-\x1F; comment stripping is single-pass and non-nesting.

flags.message: The claimed bypass using nested comments like 'expr/**/ession(' is incorrect; comment stripping removes '/**/' and yields 'expression(', which is detected.
flags.evidence: _substitute_comments removes the '/*...*/' pattern, so 'expr/**/ession(' becomes 'expression(' before the 'expression(' check, causing _has_sneaky_javascript to return True.

sanity_check.reasoning: The finding points to a real weakness in the heuristic-based CSS sanitization: the function does not decode CSS escapes and its whitespace class omits some control characters, so bypasses are possible. However, the specific example given for comment-based bypass is wrong, and the actual exploitability depends on how the library is used. Manual review is needed to confirm severity and whether the package treats this as a security boundary.

findings.description: ElementInclude._lxml_default_loader follows attacker-controlled xi:include href, enabling SSRF and local file disclosure when expanding untrusted XML
findings.reasoning: In _include(), `href = urljoin(base_url, e.get("href"))` is taken directly from the xi:include element's href attribute and passed unvalidated into _lxml_default_loader, which (a) calls urlopen(href) for any href containing "://" (SSRF: http/https/ftp/file), (b) calls open(href,'rb') for local paths (arbitrary local file read, CWE-610/CWE-611), and (c) for parse="xml" delegates to etree.parse(href, parser) which has the same effect and can also expand external entities depending on the parser. The only mitigations present are the recursion-depth limit and detection of re-included hrefs — there is no scheme allow-list, no `no_network` handling and no restriction of file:// or internal/metadata addresses. An application that expands XInclude over user-supplied XML (the documented use of this ElementInclude-compatible module) therefore allows an attacker to make the server issue requests to internal endpoints or read local files whose content can be reflected back into the resulting tree. Note this module intentionally mirrors ElementTree behaviour, so the project may consider it by-design; the mitigating factor is that exploitation requires the host application to call ElementInclude.include() on untrusted input.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Untrusted XML -> xi:include/@href -> urljoin(base_url, href) -> load_include(href, ...) -> _lxml_default_loader -> urlopen(href) / open(href,'rb') / etree.parse(href, parser). No sanitizer on scheme, host, path or network access.
evidence.notes: Only max_depth recursion limiting (DEFAULT_MAX_INCLUSION_DEPTH=6) and recursive-href detection exist; no URL/file allow-listing, no no_network flag.

flags.message: The vulnerable code is an opt-in XInclude loader. It is only exploitable if the consuming application processes attacker-controlled XML and explicitly invokes XInclude/ElementInclude.include; the package itself does not show an untrusted source reaching this path.
flags.evidence: ElementInclude._include selects _lxml_default_loader only when XInclude expansion is invoked. No in-package call with untrusted XML is provided.

flags.message: CWE-611 (XXE) is a loose fit. The core behavior is XInclude external resource resolution (SSRF/local file read), not necessarily XML external entity expansion.
flags.evidence: _lxml_default_loader uses urlopen/open for xi:include href and etree.parse(href, parser). Parser entity behavior depends on the caller-supplied parser.

sanity_check.reasoning: The code trace is accurate: href from xi:include is passed to urlopen/open/etree.parse without allowlisting. However, this is a library XInclude default loader that is only reachable when the caller opts into XInclude processing on untrusted XML, so exploitability depends on application usage. It should be reviewed rather than accepted as a clear package vulnerability.

findings.description: open_http_urllib performs urlopen on the URL taken from the parsed form's action/base_url, allowing requests to arbitrary/internal endpoints when submitting hostile HTML
findings.reasoning: The URL passed to urlopen comes from the HTML document's form action / base_url, i.e. attacker-controlled markup. An application that parses untrusted HTML and then calls form.submit() will issue a server-side request to whatever URL the document specifies (including internal addresses such as 169.254.169.254 or localhost). The code even carries a FIXME acknowledging there is no scheme/relative-URL validation. This is inherent API behavior documented in the docstring (users can pass open_http), so it is a design-level SSRF risk requiring consumer-side review rather than a blunt bug.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Attacker HTML -> form action attribute -> lxml.html.FormElement -> submit_form() -> open_http_urllib() -> urlopen(url) (no scheme/host allow-list).
evidence.notes: Documented feature; exploitable only if the consuming application submits forms parsed from untrusted input.

flags.message: This is a caller-responsibility issue, not a direct library vulnerability. lxml.html does not automatically fetch URLs from parsed HTML; the application must explicitly call form.submit()/submit_form() on attacker-controlled markup.
flags.evidence: submit_form() is an explicit API. The URL is intentionally derived from form.action/base_url, and open_http_urllib() is the default HTTP opener. The finding itself notes exploitability only if the consuming application submits forms from untrusted input.

flags.message: The lack of scheme/host validation is a hardening concern for a convenience HTTP submitter, but not a standalone SSRF vulnerability in the library.
flags.evidence: The FIXME mentions testing for relative URLs, not blocking internal hosts. No automatic network request occurs without the caller invoking the submit API.

sanity_check.reasoning: The code path described is real: form.action/base_url flows to urlopen() when a caller explicitly submits a parsed form. However, this is documented and intended library behavior, not an inherent vulnerability. findings.description: XInclude default loader opens an XML-document-controlled path (arbitrary local file read / path traversal)
findings.code_snippet:

findings.reasoning: `default_loader` is the ET-compatible XInclude resource loader. Its only argument, `href`, is fully attacker-controlled when the caller expands an untrusted XML document: `_include()` computes `href = urljoin(base_url, e.get("href"))` from the `href` attribute of the `xi:include` element in the document, then invokes the loader. There is no restriction to a base directory, no scheme check and no canonicalisation, so a document containing `<xi:include href="/etc/passwd" parse="text"/>` (or `../../../../etc/shadow`) makes the library read arbitrary files off the host filesystem and splice their contents into the tree/text output. The query's path from the XML attribute to `open()` is direct and unmitigated for this loader (this loader is used when a caller passes `loader=ElementInclude.default_loader`, and it is also reachable through `_wrap_et_loader`). Because `href` is derived from document content rather than host code, this is a genuine CWE-22/CWE-611 arbitrary-file-read primitive for any application that expands untrusted XML.

findings.description: _lxml_default_loader opens/fetches an XML-document-controlled href (arbitrary file read + SSRF) for parse="text" XIncludes
findings.reasoning: `_lxml_default_loader` is the loader actually used by `_include()` when no explicit loader is supplied (`load_include = _lxml_default_loader`). Its `href` comes straight from the `href` attribute of the `xi:include` element in the parsed document (`href = urljoin(base_url, e.get(\"href\"))`), so it is attacker-controlled whenever untrusted XML is expanded. In the `parse="text"` branch the code only checks whether the string contains `://`: a value containing `://` is fetched with `urlopen()` (SSRF to internal services / cloud metadata), anything else is passed to `open()` (arbitrary local file read, e.g. `href="/etc/passwd"` or `href="../../../../etc/shadow"`). There is no base-directory confinement, no scheme allow-list, and no canonicalisation. In the `parse="xml"` branch `etree.parse(href, parser)` reuses the document's parser and can likewise dereference remote/local resources. This is the default code path used by `ElementInclude.include(elem)` and therefore the highest-impact instance in this file.

findings.description: XInclude default loader opens an attacker-controllable href path, allowing local file disclosure / path traversal via crafted xi:include elements
